rationale: I own this one, and an 8-day-old position that is down 7.42% tells me nothing about the business. A falling price is not a sell trigger when the moat is intact. The snapshot shows a 5-year average ROE of 26.9%, debt-to-equity of 0.32, and a price well below the model's $437.57 owner-earnings value. But that value rests on 8% growth and a 5% discount rate, and I would not bet the farm on a model that sensitive. My real worry is whether the moat, a consulting franchise built on client relationships, survives rapid technological change, because moats that must be rebuilt constantly are no moats at all. The snapshot has no 10-year earnings record, CEO tenure or ROIC, so I keep the position but add nothing until I can check those.

rationale: We own six shares, bought yesterday, so the question is whether to keep them, and nothing in the numbers tells me to sell. Five-year owner earnings average about $1.57 billion, and on a zero-growth, 5% discount-rate DCF that gives roughly $117.52 a share against a $97.29 price, a 17.2% margin of safety. That clears my 15% bar, but not by much. The 48.35% average ROE looks wonderful, yet I distrust it, because I can't tell from this snapshot how much comes from a small equity base. Debt-to-equity of 0.37 is acceptable. My real worry is the moat: selling electronics against Amazon and the manufacturers themselves is a scale business, not a See's Candies, and the snapshot gives me no margin or retention data to prove otherwise. So I hold a small position, don't add on a one-day-old thesis, and sell only if the franchise test fails or the price runs well past intrinsic value.

rationale: I own this one, and I'm going to keep it, though only a day in, so I'm not pretending to have learned anything new. A service business whose moat rests on sticky client relationships can be eroded by rapid technological change, and I've been burned by moats that had to be rebuilt every year. So I hold a small position, add only if the evidence on durability firms up, and sell if the franchise test fails.

rationale: I own this one, down about 16% from my $128.38 entry, and a falling price alone is no reason to sell if the franchise is intact. rationale: I don't own Adobe, and the numbers in front of me are attractive: a five-year average ROE of about 40%, debt-to-equity of 0.41, and a computed margin of safety of 50% against a $467.50 estimate. But that estimate rests on a 5% discount rate and 8% growth, and a value that big deserves suspicion before I trust it. My real hesitation is the moat. Creative software has switching costs, but I can't tell from this snapshot whether customers are as sticky as they were, and I don't know what rapid change in AI-generated content does to that stickiness. This snapshot has no ten-year earnings record, no retention data and no management detail, and what I can't check hasn't passed. So I watch, and I'll want a clearer view of whether the moat is structural or must be rebuilt every year before I put real money behind it.

rationale: I own this one, and I'm keeping it. That is an 18.2% margin of safety, which clears my 15% bar without asking the future to do anything heroic. I'm not pretending this is See's Candies, though. Selling cars and trucks is a thin-margin, cyclical trade, and the moat is mostly franchise protections and scale, which is a modest one at best. I'm down 1.87% on a 109-day-old position, and a price dip with the business intact is no reason to sell. But I can't add aggressively until I see ten years of earnings and the management record, and this snapshot doesn't give me either.

rationale: We own a small piece of General Dynamics, and I'm content to keep it. The snapshot puts intrinsic value at $417.44 a share against a price of $352.94, a 15.45% margin of safety. That clears my 15% bar, but only just, so I would not be adding aggressively here. Five-year average ROE is 17.17% and debt-to-equity is 0.30, which is the kind of return on capital without leverage I like to see. The franchise rests on submarines and defense programs where the customer is a government with very few alternatives, and that is hard to dislodge. I can't verify the ten-year earnings record or management tenure from this snapshot, so my confidence stays moderate. I'll hold, let time work, and sell only if the moat erodes.
